title: Police shootings tragic but inevitable
article: As disturbing as it is, to the families of the victims and to the public in general, to see the use of force by police in recent weeks, there are times when there is no other choice for officers but to shoot.

Saskatchewan has been the scene of three police shootings in recent weeks. In Ile-a-la-Crosse, Roydan Morin was wounded as police surrounded a home and tried to subdue him. As he approached officers armed with a knife, a shot was fired. He is now recovering from that wound and is facing charges in court.

Not so fortunate was Melvin Bigsky, who was pulled over by police on a highway near Saskatoon on suspicion of drunken driving. The situation escalated with the police car being rammed and Bigsky continuing to threaten the officer despite the use of pepper spray, a baton and handcuffs to try to subdue him. In the end, a shot was fired. Bigsky died.

And this past weekend, a call to a home in the Saskatoon area began a chase that ended in death as well. Keldon McMillan was to be arrested on firearms charges in connection with an incident involving his estranged wife. When police approached his home, he attempted to escape the police. Two spike belts didn't stop him. Neither could a police dog; McMillan shot and killed the dog. Finally, as his handgun was raised again and pointed toward the officers, the police shot back. McMillan died.
Each case raises questions about the use of force. Those questions, however, must be applied to both sides of the equation, not just the police.

One man used a knife, another a vehicle and the third a handgun to threaten the lives of police officers as well as civilians. Whatever the reasons behind these actions -- drugs, alcohol, depression -- the threat of violence in this way cannot allowed to continue. Police officers will do all that they can to stop and disarm the person, but in the end must protect themselves and the public from danger. Sometimes, tragically, that means death.

Investigations into these incidents may find further information that can guide officers in future situations like these, leading to happier endings. The investigations may also find -- simply and sadly -- that there was no other choice to be made. Even with the best negotiation techniques and interventions, sometimes there is only one outcome.
